skyline.text: Pinker’s para­ble of two farm­ers, and why poverty mat­ters more
An econ­o­mist asks why elites pre­fer be­liefs that cost noth­ing
The words he left out, and the ver­sion pro­test­ers held up

brief.head: Staring at the pedals
brief.text: Spotify led Amit Varma to shoegaze, named for gui­tarists who stared at their ef­fects ped­als, and to Galaxie 500, the ear­lier band of Luna’s Dean Wareham. {046-S01}

brief.head: Stuck in 1992
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s first an­swer to “what are the two most re­cent songs that you know?” was *November Rain*[[x4]]. Thinking harder, he found one from 2017 and one from 2018. {046-S02}

brief.head: Instant opinions
brief.text: Amit Varma bris­tles at peo­ple who think about a sub­ject for thirty sec­onds and tweet a ver­dict[[x5]]. He has read about it for thirty years, he said. {046-J13}

brief.head: Bootleggers love bans
brief.text: Bruce Yandle’s in­sight[[x6]]: the moral­ist de­mand­ing a ban and the boot­leg­ger prof­it­ing from it want the same thing, so the boot­leg­ger funds the pro­hi­bi­tion­ist politi­cian[[x7]]. {046-C07}

brief.head: Cronies need not apply
brief.text: Pro-business and pro-market can mean op­po­site[[x8]] things, Amit Varma said. Businesses ally with the state to keep com­peti­tors out; free mar­kets make serv­ing peo­ple the only route. {046-C08}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: Those who sig­nal the most virtue pos­sess the least.
thought.who: Amit Varma, a maxim he often repeats, found especially true of men[[x9]]

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on beliefs that hurt the poor
lead.head: Rich man’s virtue, poor man’s bill

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 46

body: It is fash­ion­able, Amit Varma said, to hold opin­ions that make you feel vir­tu­ous while the poor pay. He calls them lux­ury be­liefs, a term from the thinker Rob Henderson, whose def­i­ni­tion he read out.
“Luxury be­liefs are ideas and opin­ions that con­fer sta­tus on the upper class while often in­flict­ing costs on the lower classes.” {046-C01}

Varma pic­tured the be­liev­ers: elites in air-conditioned liv­ing rooms, typ­ing into MacBooks, choos­ing which lux­ury head­phones to add to the three they al­ready have, and propos­ing poli­cies that hurt the poor.

His an­ti­dote is Gandhi’s test, which both hosts take in­spi­ra­tion from: be­fore any pol­icy, ask first what it does to the poor. In a coun­try as poor as India, Varma said, that is a moral ques­tion.
He and Ajay Shah then worked through five such be­liefs, mostly from the left, one plainly from the right, and asked why com­fort­able peo­ple hold them.
## Five fash­ion­able mis­takes

Socialism, Varma said, is not a word for car­ing about so­ci­ety. It means a state that owns much of the prop­erty and reg­u­lates the rest, where free­dom is some­thing granted. His lens is con­sent against co­er­cion, and so­cial­ism, he said, is co­er­cion. {046-C02}

Inequality is the wrong tar­get. In a pos­i­tive-sum world, growth makes the poor richer and the rich richer still, so poverty can fall as in­equal­ity rises, as it did after 1991. Would you rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh?
Banning vic­tim­less crimes, the right’s con­tri­bu­tion, hands pros­ti­tu­tion, bet­ting and liquor to the un­der­world, where the rule of law does not reach.

Anti-capitalism scorns the sweat­shop that is, for the per­son work­ing in it, the best op­tion on offer. And price con­trols throw away the in­for­ma­tion prices carry, so that scarcity al­ways fol­lows.
## The arith­metic of pa­tience

Shah added num­bers. A growth-hostile pol­icy setup, he sug­gested, gives India about 2 per cent per capita growth; a pro-growth one about 4 per cent. At 2 per cent, in­comes take 70 years to quadru­ple. At 4 per cent, they take 32.
“You think only 200 basis points,” he said, “but there’s a power of com­pound­ing.” {046-C05}
Varma put it in peo­ple: every one per cent rise in GDP, he said, gets about two mil­lion Indians out of poverty.
## Why the com­fort­able be­lieve

Shah, “a card car­ry­ing econ­o­mist”, asked what the elites are op­ti­mis­ing for. Pious views, he sug­gested, cost noth­ing once you are rich, buy safety from pitch­forks and a pop­ulist state, and sig­nal mem­ber­ship of a club.
“To buy a Louis Vuitton is at least ex­pen­sive,” he said. “Here it’s talk. Talk is free.” {046-C11}
Varma was more gen­er­ous. Most be­liev­ers mean well, he said; they sig­nal virtue to them­selves as much as to oth­ers. Social media then re­wards tribes, pu­rity tests and dou­bling down.
He read from Thomas Sowell’s *The Vision of the Anointed* to show that the habit is old: those who dis­agree with the pre­vail­ing vi­sion are seen as being “not merely in error, but in sin”.
Shah warned busi­ness elites who court the strong­man that pop­ulists have often turned on their rich back­ers.

Varma closed by rec­om­mend­ing Walter Block’s *Defending the Undefendable*, and with some ad­vice. “When it comes to val­ues, be firm on your val­ues,” he said. “When it comes to the facts of the world, the world is deeply com­plex. Be open, lis­ten to peo­ple who dis­agree with you.” {046-C14}

second.label: Degrowth
second.head: Degrowth on the rocks
second.deck: A partygoer with a single malt meets Amit Varma’s arithmetic of poverty

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the degrowth enthusiast

body: At a party a few days be­fore the record­ing, Amit Varma met a very suc­cess­ful pro­fes­sional from Hyderabad. Sipping a sin­gle malt, the man said he found the word “de­growth” very at­trac­tive: India, he felt, had had enough growth. {046-S08}
Varma told him that free speech was fine, but that what he was say­ing was deeply im­moral. Growth, Varma said, is what gets[[x1]] peo­ple out of poverty.

Over the last 30 years, he said, every one per cent rise in GDP has got two mil­lion Indians out of poverty. {#twomillion} To those who have es­caped poverty, it is a num­ber. To Varma, it is two mil­lion human be­ings who can live bet­ter lives.

quote.text: Free speech is fine and please say what­ever you want, but ev­ery­thing you’re say­ing is deeply im­moral be­cause de­growth hurts the poor.

third.head: The strongman bites back

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the strongman’s rich backers

body: Business lead­ers who have skimped on un­der­stand­ing so­ci­ety, Ajay Shah said, often make an in­tel­lec­tual error. They seek out the strong­man[[x2]] and col­lab­o­rate with him, sure that he will de­liver the goods. {#strongman}
In Saudi Arabia, MBS led a shake­down of hun­dreds of rich peo­ple. In China, Xi Jinping partly de­stroyed and partly ex­pro­pri­ated[[x3]] the rich. In Russia, Putin went after them.

“Each in­di­vid­ual bil­lion­aire at some point thought that no, no, no, I’m the in­sider, I will get spe­cial favours by the gov­ern­ment, and for some time it seems to work,” Shah said. “But in steady state it didn’t.” {046-S09}
Populist lead­ers, he said, have often been bad for eco­nomic growth in gen­eral. The only sus­tain­able path for build­ing firms, in his view, is rule of law and lib­eral democ­racy.

p2.title: Five luxury beliefs
p2.deck: Socialism, inequality, bans, anti-capitalism and price controls: five opinions that flatter the comfortable and hurt the poor

from1.head: Rich man’s virtue, poor man’s bill

quote.text: I care deeply about con­sent. It has an ab­so­lute value. And so­cial­ism is equal to co­er­cion.

box.title: Where the phrase comes from
box.text: Rob Henderson, whom Amit Varma calls a very fine thinker worth fol­low­ing, coined the term “lux­ury be­liefs”. His new book, *Troubled*, is about grow­ing up in fos­ter homes, and Varma rec­om­mends it highly. {046-R07}

sections.label: Belief One
sections.head: Subjects, not citizens
sections.caption: socialism as coercion
body: Many peo­ple hear “so­cial­ism” as mean­ing what is good for so­ci­ety, Amit Varma said, just as pop­ulism is con­fused with pop­u­lar. It is a deeply toxic word.[[x10]]

His def­i­ni­tion is stricter. The state owns a lot of the prop­erty and reg­u­lates the rest; in­di­vid­ual lib­erty is frowned upon. “You are not a cit­i­zen, you are a sub­ject,” he said. Freedom is not the de­fault con­di­tion but some­thing granted by the state. {046-C02}

Guests on his pod­cast *The Seen and the Unseen* who are now in their fifties and six­ties, he said, talk fondly of the good old days of so­cial­ism. They were elite then and are elite now. Yet so­cial­ism, Varma said, kept hun­dreds of mil­lions poor for decades longer than nec­es­sary.
## Marx’s check­list

Ajay Shah sug­gested an ex­er­cise. *The Communist Manifesto* by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels ends with a check­list, a pro­gramme for ac­tion, and you will be as­ton­ished, he said, at how much of it is in mod­ern India. {046-R11}
Communism, Varma replied, is about state co­er­cion and cen­tral­is­ing power, and India has seen a lot of that for all its 75-plus years.

~ Why is the idea fash­ion­able again? A young gen­er­a­tion, Varma said, feels vir­tu­ous at the thought of using the state to do good for so­ci­ety, with­out car­ing about the un­seen cost, and has not seen the hor­rors of so­cial­ism.

quote.text: I care deeply about con­sent. It has an ab­so­lute value. And so­cial­ism is equal to co­er­cion.

portraits.caption: Karl Marx
portraits.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain

sections.label: Belief Two
sections.head: Mind the poverty, not the gap
sections.caption: poverty versus inequality
body: Inequality, Amit Varma ar­gued, is a fash­ion of the West that India can­not af­ford while it has poverty to solve. In a zero-sum world, poverty and in­equal­ity would move to­gether. In a pos­i­tive-sum world, growth spreads across the spec­trum: the poor get richer, the rich get richer still, and in­equal­ity goes up.
That, he said, is what hap­pened after 1991, when hun­dreds of mil­lions of peo­ple came out of poverty. {#liberalisation}
His test: would you rather be poor in the USA[[x11]][[x12]], which has greater in­equal­ity, or in Bangladesh, which has greater poverty? Everybody, he said, an­swers the USA. {046-C03}

He drew on the philoso­pher Harry Frankfurt’s slim book *On Inequality* and its doc­trine of suf­fi­ciency: de­fine what is enough to live on, and get ev­ery­one there. Every Indian gov­ern­ment, Varma said, has failed at that. {046-C04}
## Two hun­dred basis points

Ajay Shah an­swered the wise se­nior peo­ple who had told him that a lit­tle chas­ing of in­equal­ity would do lit­tle harm to growth. At 2 per cent per capita growth, he said, in­comes dou­ble in 35 years; at 4 per cent, in about 16. {#ruleof70}

~ Thirty-two years, the time to quadru­ple at 4 per cent, is within the plan­ning hori­zon of the show’s ed­i­tor, Nomsita, Shah noted. “Thirty-two years later she’ll be younger than you are now,” Varma said.

quote.text: The doc­trine of suf­fi­ciency is that you de­fine what is enough for a man to live on.

sections.label: Belief Three
sections.head: Ban it, and the mob moves in
sections.caption: victimless crimes
body: The third be­lief comes from the right, Amit Varma said: pros­ti­tu­tion is bad, ban it; bet­ting breeds match-fixing, ban it; al­co­hol is a so­cial evil, ban it. The bans do not end these trades. They hand them to the un­der­world, where the cops are paid off and the rule of law does not apply.[[x13]]

In the Netherlands, he said, pros­ti­tu­tion is legal, broth­els are reg­u­lated and ad­ver­tise openly, sex work­ers have rights and pay taxes, and the level of crime against them is re­ally low. {#netherlands}

He re­called a talk show hosted by Barkha Dutt on which Kiran Bedi was moral­is­tic about pros­ti­tu­tion. Sex work­ers on the show pushed back: they had got into it will­ingly, as the best op­tion open to them. {046-S05}
## The bootlegger’s friend
Varma would make bet­ting legal and tax it, as England does, charg­ing the houses rather than the gamblers’ win­nings. He wants banks to offer bet­ting the way they offer demat ac­counts.
He cited the econ­o­mist Bruce Yandle’s essay on boot­leg­gers and Baptists[[x14]]: the moral­ist call­ing for a ban and the boot­leg­ger prof­it­ing from it want the same thing. {046-C07}
~ His rule is sim­ple: con­sent­ing adults should be free to do what­ever they want with each other, as long as they harm no one else. {046-C06}

quote.text: We chose it as a best op­tion open to us, and you let us make our de­ci­sions.
quote.who: Sex workers on a TV panel, as recalled by Amit Varma

sections.label: Belief Four
sections.head: Tweeting against capitalism
sections.caption: capitalism and its critics
body: Anti-capitalism, Amit Varma said, is the pre­serve of both left and right in India. Its be­liev­ers sit in air-conditioned liv­ing rooms, tweet­ing on a cap­i­tal­ist plat­form about late cap­i­tal­ism. So many peo­ple who rant against Amazon, he added, will also order from Amazon. {#amazon}

Capitalism does turn ugly when it is aligned with power, he con­ceded. That is crony cap­i­tal­ism, in which a busi­ness uses the state to keep com­pe­ti­tion out. Pro-business and pro-market, he said, can mean op­po­site things. {046-C08}
In true free mar­kets, the state does lit­tle be­yond up­hold­ing the rule of law, so the only way to make money is by serv­ing peo­ple.
## In de­fence of sweat­shops
Sweatshops, Varma said, are amaz­ing. Nobody wants any­one to work in one, but the per­son who does is there be­cause it is the best op­tion open to them[[x15]]. {046-C09}

Child labour is hor­ri­ble, he agreed. But blunt bans pushed from Western coun­tries have sent laid-off chil­dren into pros­ti­tu­tion and crime. Studies by Kaushik Basu, Alan Krueger and Eric Edmonds try to work out the fam­ily in­come above which chil­dren stop being sent to work. The long-term so­lu­tion is growth.
~ The new­est fash­ion he de­spises is de­growth, which, he said, hurts the poor.

quote.text: Those peo­ple chose to work in a sweat­shop be­cause it was the best op­tion open to them. Respect their agency, re­spect their de­ci­sion.

sections.label: Belief Five
sections.head: No car above Rs 10,000
sections.caption: price controls
body: Amit Varma has spo­ken about price con­trols so often, he said, that you could print it on T-shirts. The elite be­lief runs: this is too ex­pen­sive, put a price con­trol on it.

He of­fered a thought ex­per­i­ment. Suppose the gov­ern­ment de­cided that every Indian should have a car, and capped cars at ten thou­sand ru­pees[[x16]]. {#tenthousand} He told view­ers to pause the video and think, and froze on cam­era him­self. {046-J07}
Cars that can­not be made for that sum, which is all of them, would dis­ap­pear, he said. The few that exist would sell on the black mar­ket, and the in­dus­try would die.
## The lost sig­nal
A price, Varma said, sig­nals the scarci­ties and con­straints of the world, and car­ries an in­cen­tive to pro­duce more. Take that in­for­ma­tion away and scarcity fol­lows. {046-C10}
It is not hy­po­thet­i­cal. When stents came under price con­trol a few years back, he tweeted that there would be scarcity. There was, and peo­ple died. {#stents}

~ Ban Uber’s surge pric­ing[[x17]] and there is no car when you must reach a hos­pi­tal or catch a flight. Such con­trols fol­low the *Yes Minister* line he quoted: we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, let’s do it.

quote.text: If you take that in­for­ma­tion away, you are al­ways going to have scarci­ties.

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Virtue at no extra cost
sections.caption: why elites hold luxury beliefs
body: Ajay Shah asked the economist’s ques­tion: what are the elites op­ti­mis­ing for? The cyn­i­cal an­swer is that once you are rich, es­pous­ing views that harm the poor costs you noth­ing.

Pious talk, he sug­gested, is an old kind of phi­lan­thropy that buys safety from folks with pitch­forks and from a pop­ulist state. {#pitchforks} It also makes you look car­ing, and it is a cheap way to claim mem­ber­ship of a club. {046-C11}

Timur Kuran’s idea of pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion[[x18]][[x19]] fits too, Shah said: peo­ple say what they think will help them get ahead. And all of it needs in­tel­lec­tual soft-headedness, a broad base of doc­tor-engineer ca­pa­bil­i­ties with very low knowl­edge of so­cial sci­ence and hu­man­i­ties. {#doctors}
## It was al­ways thus

Amit Varma cred­ited most be­liev­ers with good in­ten­tions: we lie to our­selves as much as to oth­ers, he said. Social media then re­wards tribes and dou­bling down. At 17 he read Marx and Engels and said silly things; with screen­shots, he might never have out­grown them. {046-C12}
But, he said, it was al­ways thus. He read from Thomas Sowell’s *The Vision of the Anointed*, sub­ti­tled *Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy*. {046-C13}
~ Shah closed with a warn­ing for busi­ness elites who back the strong­man: in Saudi Arabia, China and Russia, the strong­man turned on the rich.

quote.text: Those who dis­agree with the pre­vail­ing vi­sion are seen as being not merely in error, but in sin.
quote.who: Thomas Sowell, as read by Amit Varma

portraits.credit: Internet Archive Book Images, public domain

quote.text: Then I feel the in­cen­tive to dou­ble down on them for ego rea­sons, and then I be­come that per­son. I don’t have that in­tel­lec­tual growth I might oth­er­wise have.

p3.title: Good intentions
p3.deck: Goats, preambles, railway stations and carpets: what each story teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the CAA protests and a word in the preamble
stories.head: Whose Constitution is it anyway?
body: During the protests against the CAA, young peo­ple across India took to the streets hold­ing up the Preamble of the Constitution. Amit Varma, who sup­ported the protests and op­poses the CAA, said it gave him great hope that the young were not ap­a­thetic.
It also filled him with de­spair. {046-S04} The pre­am­ble they held up was Indira’s, not Ambedkar’s, and Indira’s has the word “so­cial­ist” in it.
He un­der­stood why. That ver­sion also has the word “sec­u­lar”, which both hosts be­lieve in, and in today’s times, he said, one could argue it has res­o­nance.

But when the two words were de­bated in Ambedkar’s time, Varma said, Ambedkar’s an­swer was no[[x20]]. On “sec­u­lar”, his rea­son­ing was that if the value is in­scribed in every ar­ti­cle of the Constitution, there is no need to state it: that is just sig­nalling.
On “so­cial­ist”, his an­swer was that the choice of eco­nomic or­gan­i­sa­tion is a ques­tion for pol­i­tics, not the Constitution. Let the po­lit­i­cal process fig­ure it out.

Ambedkar him­self favoured a so­cial­is­tic form of or­gan­i­sa­tion then, Varma said, but by the 1950s he had changed his mind: “a great thinker who con­tained mul­ti­tudes”. The Dalit thinker Chandra Bhan Prasad once told Varma that his he­roes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, and Varma sus­pects Ambedkar would have ap­proved.
~ Socialism, Varma in­sisted, is not a harm­less word mean­ing the good of so­ci­ety. {#harmless} It im­plies state co­er­cion and cen­tral­i­sa­tion, and it was writ­ten into the Constitution.
stories.why: Ambedkar, Varma said, was a great thinker who con­tained mul­ti­tudes and changed his mind, so one has to see his full body of work. And the fash­ion­able read­ing of the Constitution qui­etly car­ries a word that, in Varma’s view, kept India poor.
stories.postscript: Varma rec­om­mends his *The Seen and the Unseen* episodes with Srinath Raghavan on the CAA, and with Chandra Bhan Prasad.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a parable from Steven Pinker
stories.head: Igor’s idea of fairness
body: Two Russian farm­ers, Boris and Igor, star in a para­ble Amit Varma took from Steven Pinker’s *Enlightenment Now*. Boris has a goat. Igor does not.
Igor goes to the au­thor­ity and com­plains that it is not fair. Asked what he wants done, he says: kill Boris’s goat[[x21]]. {046-S03}
That, Varma said, is the end of in­equal­ity. And now nei­ther of them has a goat. He thinks about the story often.

~ Later he re­turned to it. The re­dis­trib­u­tor takes Boris’s goat, cuts it in half and gives a half each to Boris and Igor. {#halfgoat} He thinks he has solved both men’s prob­lems, Varma said, and feels vir­tu­ous. But to­mor­row nei­ther has a goat.
stories.why: How you treat in­equal­ity, Varma said, is by killing Boris’s goat: you make both peo­ple equally poor. How you treat poverty is through eco­nomic growth, which in a poor coun­try will in­evitably raise in­equal­ity. That, he said, is fine.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Boris, Igor and the goat

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Section 377 and a police racket
stories.head: Next station: extortion
body: Years ago, Amit Varma wrote a col­umn called *The Matunga Racket*[[x22]]. {046-R20} It de­scribed what some cops did while Section 377 made ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity ef­fec­tively il­le­gal in India.

They placed ads on on­line bul­letin boards, ask­ing gay men to come and spend time with them. The men would go to the rail­way sta­tion in ques­tion, often Matunga, where plain­clothes cops met them.
Then came the ex­tor­tion. The cops threat­ened to tell the man’s fam­ily, his wife or his fa­ther. “And they’d go with him to the ATM, they’d use his card, they’d empty it out.” {046-S06}
~ It was a re­ally com­mon racket, Varma said. Section 377 has since, thank­fully, been struck down, and that can­not hap­pen now.
stories.why: A law against a vic­tim­less crime, Varma ar­gued, does not just fail: it hands its own en­forcers a tool against harm­less peo­ple. His prin­ci­ple is that con­sent­ing adults should be free to do what­ever they want, as long as they harm no one else. {046-C06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Matunga racket

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what happened after the bans
stories.head: Saved from work, lost to worse
body: In Bangladesh, after Western ac­tivists com­plained about al­leged sweat­shops, 30,000 chil­dren were laid off[[x23]]. {#oxfam} Oxfam fol­lowed up, Amit Varma said: many of the girls went into pros­ti­tu­tion, and many of the boys turned to crime.
In Nepal, a scan­dal over chil­dren mak­ing car­pets led to 5,000 to 7,000 chil­dren being laid off. A UNICEF study found that the girls prac­ti­cally uni­formly went into pros­ti­tu­tion. {#nepal}
No par­ent wants a child in a fac­tory, Varma said. Families send chil­dren to work be­cause every other op­tion is worse. Good schools need pros­per­ity, and pros­per­ity needs growth.
~ The jour­nal­ists who write such sto­ries, he said, never fol­low up. The cam­paign­ers feel vir­tu­ous and for­get, and the children’s lives can be­come hell.

quote.text: There is no par­ent in the world who wants a child to work in a fac­tory or a sweat­shop.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the children laid off

quiz.q: In Steven Pinker’s parable, what does Igor ask the authority to do about Boris’s goat?
quiz.a: Kill it: in­equal­ity ends, and nei­ther farmer has a goat.

quiz.q: Would you rather be poor in the USA or in Bangladesh, and what does the answer show?
quiz.a: The USA: it is more un­equal, but poverty, not in­equal­ity, is what mat­ters.

quiz.q: At 4 per cent per capita growth, how long do incomes take to quadruple?
quiz.a: About 32 years, by the rule of 70, against 70 years at 2 per cent.

quiz.q: Which two words did Ambedkar decline to put in the preamble, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Secular and so­cial­ist: one was mere sig­nalling, the other a ques­tion for pol­i­tics.

quiz.q: What happened when stents were put under price control, according to Varma?
quiz.a: Scarcities of stents, as he had tweeted there would be, and peo­ple died.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s analysis, why are luxury beliefs cheaper than a Louis Vuitton?
quiz.a: Because they are only talk, and talk is free, yet they sig­nal club mem­ber­ship.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 46. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Thomas Sowell (Internet Archive Book Images, public domain); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple, Open Library, Spotify and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Nowhere Near
shelf.creator: Yo La Tengo
shelf.why: He calls it a beau­ti­ful song and one of the great love songs.

shelf.title: On Fire
shelf.creator: Galaxie 500
shelf.why: He calls it a bril­liant album you’ve got to lis­ten to, an old love fi­nally found.

shelf.title: Lunapark
shelf.creator: Luna
shelf.why: He calls it a great album from a band he loved.

shelf.title: November Rain
shelf.creator: Guns N’ Roses
shelf.why: A 1992 song that marks where his mu­si­cal sense of ‘recent’ had stopped.

shelf.title: Sign of the Times
shelf.creator: Harry Styles
shelf.why: A song he gen­uinely loves, and Harry Styles is called ‘bloody good’.

shelf.title: Shallow
shelf.creator: Lady Gaga and Bradley Cooper
shelf.why: One of the only re­cent songs Ajay knows and loves.

shelf.title: Troubled: A Memoir of Foster Care, Family, and Social Class
shelf.creator: Rob Henderson
shelf.why: Highly rec­om­mended.

shelf.title: Luxury Beliefs are Status Symbols
shelf.creator: Rob Henderson
shelf.why: Gives the orig­i­nal fram­ing: be­liefs that con­fer sta­tus on the upper class while in­flict­ing costs on the lower classes.

shelf.title: Enlightenment Now
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Shows vividly why chas­ing equal­ity can mean mak­ing ev­ery­one poorer.

shelf.title: On Inequality
shelf.creator: Harry Frankfurt
shelf.why: A slim, great book that sets out the ‘doc­trine of sufficiency’: de­fine what is enough to live on and get ev­ery­one there.

shelf.title: The Communist Manifesto
shelf.creator: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
shelf.why: Ajay re­jects its pre­scrip­tions but finds whole chunks ‘ab­so­lutely brilliant’ on how cap­i­tal­ism and glob­al­i­sa­tion would tear up the feu­dal order.

shelf.title: The Vision of the Anointed: Self-Congratulation as a Basis for Social Policy
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: A great book whose sub­ti­tle sums up the episode.

shelf.title: Defending the Undefendable
shelf.creator: Walter Block
shelf.why: Block, an Austrian econ­o­mist, de­fends ideas con­sid­ered be­yond the pale, much as Amit has just de­fended sweat­shops and legal pros­ti­tu­tion.

shelf.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: The Education of a Regulatory Economist
shelf.creator: Bruce Yandle
shelf.why: Yandle’s ‘beau­ti­ful way of think­ing about how reg­u­la­tion works’: the moral cru­sader (the Baptist) and the black-market sup­plier (the boot­leg­ger) both want the ban, so they lobby for the same end, some­times with the boot­leg­ger fund­ing the Baptist.

shelf.title: The Economics of Child Labor
shelf.creator: Kaushik Basu and Pham Hoang Van
shelf.why: Calls it a great study.

shelf.title: Observations on International Labor Standards and Trade
shelf.creator: Alan B Krueger
shelf.why: Calls it an­other great study on the eco­nom­ics of child labour.

shelf.title: Child Labor in the Global Economy
shelf.creator: Eric V Edmonds and Nina Pavcnik
shelf.why: Calls it an­other great study sup­port­ing the case that pros­per­ity, not bans, ends child labour.

shelf.title: Why Children Labour
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Gives the full ar­gu­ment and ev­i­dence, in­clud­ing the Oxfam Bangladesh and UNICEF Nepal fol­low-ups.

shelf.title: Laws Against Victimless Crimes Should Be Scrapped
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that ban­ning pros­ti­tu­tion, bet­ting and al­co­hol only hands these ac­tiv­i­ties to the un­der­world.

shelf.title: The Matunga Racket
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A con­crete case of how crim­i­nal­is­ing con­sent­ing adults turns a vic­tim­less ‘crime’ into a tool for po­lice ex­tor­tion.

shelf.title: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s re­view ar­gu­ing that the film gets pro­hi­bi­tion eco­nom­ics back­wards: a real boot­leg­ger would fund the anti-alcohol politi­cian, not fight him, be­cause their in­cen­tives are aligned.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: India’s Problem is Poverty, Not Inequality
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit sep­a­rates two prob­lems peo­ple rou­tinely con­fuse and that need op­po­site so­lu­tions: in a pos­i­tive-sum world in­equal­ity can rise while poverty falls, as in India after 1991, so end­ing poverty through growth is the real moral im­per­a­tive.

shelf.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Episode 45)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Populism is not ‘what is popular’ but a dan­ger­ous pack­age of be­liefs and meth­ods, ris­ing world­wide along­side na­tion­al­ism, that works by in­vent­ing en­e­mies and sell­ing in­su­lar slo­gans like im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

shelf.title: Poker and Life (Episode 38)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: What Amit’s five years as a pro­fes­sional poker player taught him about life: most of what hap­pens is luck, so don’t let suc­cess go to your head or fail­ure crush you, and focus on doing the right things.

shelf.title: The Citizenship Battles (Episode 152 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
shelf.why: He calls it a great episode on the CAA.

shelf.title: Caste, Capitalism and Chandra Bhan Prasad (Episode 296 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Chandra Bhan Prasad
shelf.why: The Dalit thinker whose two he­roes are Ambedkar and Adam Smith, a pair­ing cen­tral to Amit’s hope for end­ing caste.

laughs.text: Ajay asks why they are colour-coordinated in shades of blue. Amit: ‘Well, you know, maybe we both love the blues.’

Ajay turns Amit’s Spotify dis­cov­ery into a Bayes’ the­o­rem prob­lem (work­ing back from track to genre). Amit protests: ‘Ajay, I’m talk­ing about art, I’m talk­ing about music, I’m talk­ing about the soul.’
Ajay in­tro­duces the topic: ‘there’s an English word lux­ury like Louis Vuitton and Indian ho­tels, and there is a word like be­liefs, which is like Bayes the­o­rem and trigonom­e­try.’
After Ajay picks ‘Shallow’ as his 2018 song, Amit: ‘You and I should per­form Shallow some­time. I’ll do the high parts.’
Ajay says 32 years out is a prac­ti­cal hori­zon for their ed­i­tor Nomsita. Amit: ‘Thirty-two years later she’ll be younger than you are now.’

Amit cor­rects him­self from ‘prostitutes’ to ‘sex workers’, then takes it back: ‘You and I are pros­ti­tutes, we’re sell­ing our ser­vices for money... I do a lot of things free even. So I’m even worse.’
In the price-control thought ex­per­i­ment, Amit tells view­ers to pause the video and think, then freezes on cam­era: ‘Have you paused? I just did statue...’
The run­ning ‘under my chair’ gag: Amit keeps say­ing links are in the show notes ‘under my chair’, and fi­nally won­ders aloud what else is down there.
Ajay be­gins his anal­y­sis: ‘I’m a card-carrying econ­o­mist, okay, and here is my card.’
The ‘gen­tle reader’ run­ning joke. Amit mid-sentence: ‘dear lis­tener, dear reader. We are not lis­ten­ers, we are read­ers.’
Amit on in­stant opin­ions: ‘You’ve thought about that for thirty sec­onds. I have read about it for thirty years... and we are sup­posed to, on Twitter, be on equal ground.’
Gandhi’s test, which both hosts take in­spi­ra­tion from: when­ever you think of a pol­icy, first ask what it does to the poor.

‘Hamara so­cial­ism achha tha’: Amit mim­ics older Seen and the Unseen guests nos­tal­gic for the so­cial­ist era. One guest even lamented the Soviet Union’s col­lapse, which Amit calls the best thing that hap­pened to all of us.
Yes Minister: Amit in­vokes the line ‘we must do some­thing, this is some­thing, let’s do it’ to de­scribe in­tel­lec­tu­ally lazy elite pol­i­cy­mak­ing.
Raees: Amit’s crit­i­cism of Shah Rukh Khan’s ‘ter­ri­ble film’, where the boot­leg­ger treats the pro­hi­bi­tion-seeking politi­cian as an enemy. In real life, Amit says, the boot­leg­ger funds him.
Section 377: the law that ef­fec­tively crim­i­nalised ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity, now struck down, which en­abled the Matunga ex­tor­tion racket.
Timur Kuran’s pref­er­ence fal­si­fi­ca­tion: Ajay cites it as one rea­son peo­ple pro­fess be­liefs that help them get ahead.
